source_read: PDF, pp. 259–274 (all 16 pages read; Table 1 and Figures 1–2 checked on pages rendered at 110 dpi; reference list skimmed)

claims.note: Dean et al. reproduce +19% (caudate), +16% (putamen) and r=0.92 with abstinence duration. They confirm there was no control for repeated measurement, but argue the increases are unlikely to be a test–retest artefact, citing reproducibility studies. They also describe a second small longitudinal DAT study (SPECT) that did retest controls, which the claim does not mention. Dean's timing ('again after ≥9 months of abstinence') slightly misdescribes the primary paper, where the second scan was at least 9 months after the first, at 12–17 months of abstinence. Nothing contradicts the claim.

anchors.locator: Hypothesis 5 ('MA abuse will be associated with changes in the human brain'), 2nd paragraph (left column)
anchors.extracted: Volkow et al. (2001): 5 users scanned after ≤6 months and again later; DAT +19% caudate and +16% putamen; increases correlated with duration of abstinence (r=0.92); test–DAT change relations only trends (timed gait, delayed recall, p<0.18). No repeated-measurement controls, but the reviewers judge a test–retest artefact unlikely.

Chou et al. (2007), SPECT: 5 users scanned while urine-positive and again after 2 weeks' abstinence; 7 controls retested after 1 week. DAT rose 5–38% (mean 20%) in users vs −14% to +13% in controls; groups not compared statistically; first scan during use complicates interpretation; WCST improvement correlated with DAT change.

claims.note: Dean et al. report the same thalamic +12% (relative) with no change in striatum or occipital cortex, and add that absolute regional metabolism did not change and that practice effects were not controlled. They do not comment on the test statistics. They also describe a control-retested FDG study over the first month (Berman et al., 2007), relevant context for any metabolism-recovery claim.

anchors.extracted: Wang et al. (2004): 5 users tested at <6 months and again after >1 year of abstinence; no change in absolute regional metabolism; relative thalamic metabolism +12%, not striatum or occipital cortex; thalamic change correlated with timed gait, processing speed and delayed recall changes, not immediate recall or pegboard; no control for practice effects.

Berman et al. (2007): 10 users at 5–9 days and after 4 weeks of abstinence, 12 controls retested at similar times; users had greater increases in global glucose metabolism (largest in parietal, orbitofrontal, insula, cingulate); group × reaction-time interaction not significant (p=0.53).

claims.note: Dean et al. support 'low-average to average' for group means and 'a minority impaired' (some susceptible individuals markedly impaired). They are not the source of the claim's numbers (7/27 vs 2/18; 34% vs 16%; 16th–55th percentiles), which come from other papers. They also argue against a categorical reading: mild deficits may still have functional consequences, demographically normed scores can hide lower absolute ability, and education-matched designs may understate deficits. The claim should keep those caveats in view.

anchors.extracted: Where users performed worse, group differences of 1 SD or less are common, placing mean user performance in the low-average to average range by some naming conventions; consistent with studies using published norms (Gonzalez 2004; Rippeth 2004; Simon 2010); some susceptible individuals show considerable impairment (e.g. Kalechstein 2003).
No reviewed study gave scatter plots; most significant group differences were within, often below, 1 SD, so substantial overlap between users and controls is likely.

anchors.locator: Discussion, left column 2nd paragraph to right column
anchors.extracted: Authors reject treating normed scores categorically (contra Hart et al.); low-average scores may mean lower function for people with less education; initial studies link deficits to lower everyday functional ability and unemployment (Henry 2010; Weber 2012).

In 36 users, earlier age of first use went with fewer years of education (r=−0.48) and a larger shortfall of actual vs cognitively predicted education (r=−0.42, p=0.011); authors infer education-matched comparisons may underestimate deficits.

claims.note: The controlled longitudinal evidence summarized here matches 'not established'. Two qualifications. (1) Dean et al. themselves rate the abstinence hypothesis as having 'mild support', citing two cross-sectional within-user comparisons. (2) Their account of Iudicello et al. (2010) differs from the claim's: they report a trend (p=0.06) for abstinent users impaired at baseline to improve more than relapsing users and controls whether impaired or not. The claim says impaired controls also improved. This should be checked against Iudicello et al. (2010) directly; Dean is a secondary source here. Editors' calculation recomputed: from the claim's own inputs for Simon et al. (2010) (t(37)=1.01; 18 vs 21) I get d=0.32 (Hedges g 0.32), 95% CI −0.31 to 0.96, the same as the claim. Dean gives only '0.14 SD more' and p=0.33, which agrees with those inputs but does not contain the t or the group sizes.

anchors.locator: Hypothesis 4, left column last paragraph to right column
anchors.extracted: Simon et al. (2010): tested at 4–9 days and after 1 month, controls retested; users did not improve significantly more in any domain; 0.14 SD more on the overall battery, p=0.33.

Iudicello et al. (2010): retest after about 1 year; 25 abstinent, 58 relapsed (urine-clean at testing); neither group changed significantly more than controls; post hoc trend (p=0.06) for abstinent users impaired at baseline to improve more than relapsers and controls (impaired or not); some subgroups as small as 6.
Pre–post improvements (Jaffe 2005; Volkow 2001; Wang 2004) had no retested control group; practice effects are common and can persist beyond a year.

Cross-sectional comparisons within users: Salo et al. (2009) found those abstinent ≥1 year better on Stroop than those abstinent 3 weeks–6 months; Kim et al. (2006) found >6 months better on WCST but not Stroop or Trails; Simon et al. (2004) found continuing users better on memory than abstinent users.
Authors rate the abstinence hypothesis as mildly supported: some dependent users may have suppressed cognition that improves with abstinence.

claims.note: This source supports only the last clause: the sibling study (Ersche et al., 2012) is mentioned in one parenthesis noting that most dependent participants used cocaine rather than methamphetamine. It does not report the sibling brain-structure or inhibitory-control findings, so the main sentence must be anchored in Ersche et al. (2012) itself. Dean's twin evidence (Toomey et al., 2003) bears on the 'predate use' inference from the other side: within discordant twin pairs, the stimulant-using twins still did worse on 4 of 14 tests.

anchors.extracted: Siblings discordant for stimulant dependence were compared on an inhibitory-control measure by Ersche et al. (2012), but the great majority of those participants used cocaine, not methamphetamine.

Toomey et al. (2003): 50 male twin pairs (31 MZ, 19 DZ) discordant for weekly stimulant use for ≥1 year (80% amphetamines); pairs similar in education, IQ (both 103), alcohol and other variables; users worse on 4 of 14 tests (cancellation, Trails A, finger tapping, grooved pegboard), better on one (continuous performance); no urinalysis at testing.

claims.note: Every reason the claim gives appears in this review: lower average scores, no pre-use measurement and premorbid confounding, unmatched education and other risk factors, and no controlled evidence of improvement beyond practice effects. However, the authors' own overall judgment leans the other way: the preponderance of evidence suggests methamphetamine causes mild decline, of unknown duration, in at least some users, with animal evidence weighted most heavily. The claim's 'not established' remains accurate, since the authors call the evidence indirect and dependent on future replication. But this review should be presented as a qualifying expert reading, not as plain support. They also argue that lower education may partly be a consequence of early use, which complicates treating education as a pure confounder.

anchors.extracted: Cross-sectional studies cannot separate pre-existing from drug-caused weaknesses; childhood executive deficits predict adolescent drug use (Tarter 2003, 2004); many studies did not match on premorbid IQ, education or other drug use.
Deficits in cross-sectional studies may reflect predisposing factors; not all confounds can be controlled; polysubstance use is extremely common; cross-sectional evidence alone is limited.

Authors conclude that the preponderance of evidence supports (abstract: the possibility of) mild cognitive decline caused by methamphetamine in at least some users, of unknown duration; animal evidence weighted most heavily; dose–response not supported; final validity depends on future research.
Early onset of use associated with less education than cognitive scores predict, so education differences may partly follow from use rather than precede it.

key_findings.correction: Detail: 31 monozygotic and 19 dizygotic pairs; 9 of the amphetamine users also used cocaine; no stimulant or cannabis use in the year before testing (p. 263).

Five studies, not four: DAT PET 5 users (Volkow 2001), DAT SPECT 5 users plus 7 retested controls (Chou 2007), FDG 5 users (Wang 2004), FDG 10 users plus 12 retested controls (Berman 2007), grey matter 12 users plus 12 retested controls (Morales 2012) (pp. 265–266). The uncorrected threshold (p<0.001, cluster >100 voxels) is from the Figure 1 note (p. 266).
Figure 2 prints p=0.011 for r=−0.42; the n for r=−0.48 is not stated.

reporting_issues.note: Abstract p. 259 ('possibility'); Discussion p. 268, summary p. 269 and Conclusion p. 270 ('does cause').
An interpretive critique rather than an internal inconsistency; the argument is on p. 261, the twin result on p. 263.

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2 critically low as a systematic summary agreed.

interpretation_gap.note: I would rate it moderate rather than minor, for the reasons the card itself lists: a causal conclusion built from lines of evidence that share confounds, animal evidence weighted most heavily despite the dose-translation caveats (p. 260), and abstinence support called 'mild' although both controlled longitudinal studies were null. In addition, brain changes during abstinence are called 'highly likely' to reflect direct effects of use (p. 269) on the basis of studies of 5–12 users.

missed: Chou et al. (2007) SPECT DAT study, the only DAT follow-up with retested controls (5 users scanned while urine-positive and after 2 weeks' abstinence, mean +20%; 7 controls −14% to +13%; groups not compared statistically) (p. 265). It is relevant to cl_meth_dat_recovery and not among the card's findings.
Dean et al. judge Volkow 2001b's DAT increases unlikely to be a test–retest artefact (p. 265). This is the basis for the 2013 timeline entry on the Volkow 2001b card.

Berman et al. (2007), the control-retested FDG study (10 users, 12 controls, about 4 weeks): users had greater increases in global metabolism (p. 265). Relevant to the metabolism claims and cited from Dean on the Wang 2004 and Cao 2026 cards, but not a key finding here.
Ersche et al. (2012) sibling study mentioned with the caveat that most participants used cocaine (p. 263), relevant to cl_meth_siblings.

Dean's account of Iudicello et al. (2010) says the abstinent-impaired subgroup tended to improve more than controls whether impaired or not (p. 264). This differs from the encyclopedia's abstinence claim, which says impaired controls also improved; check against the primary paper.
Minor: Dean describes the Volkow 2001b second scan as after ≥9 months of abstinence (p. 265); the primary paper has it at least 9 months after the first scan, at 12–17 months of abstinence.
